title: Biohybrid_system
summary:
Biohybrid systems refer to the integration of biological materials, such as cells or tissues, with artificial components, including electronics or mechanical structures. This combination uses the capabilities of living organisms alongside the precision of man-made technology, enabling the performance of tasks that neither biology nor machines could achieve independently. At their core, biohybrid systems work by bridging living biological parts with technological aspects, where biological parts may be cells, tissues, or even organs occasionally cultured in a laboratory setting.

Biological components include muscle cells for contraction, endothelial cells for vascularization, and stem cells for regenerative capabilities. Mechanical components comprise soft actuators that mimic organic motion, synthetic scaffolds that provide support and structure, and microfluidic systems that facilitate the delivery of nutrients and removal of waste.

Biohybrid systems may have transformative potential across multiple sectors such as robotics, to create actuators and sensors that mimic natural muscle and nerve function, and medicine, in developing smart implants and drug delivery systems. Notable research projects include Harvard researchers who developed a biohybrid swimming ray powered by rat cardiac cells layered onto a gold skeleton mimicking the motion of a real stingray, and MIT engineers who created a cardiac pump actuated entirely by living heart muscle cells simulating the behavior of a beating heart.

One of the most significant challenges is engineering interfaces between living tissue and artificial materials that are efficient, requiring precise control over adhesion at the surface, diffusion of nutrients, and signal conduction. As with many technologies that involve living systems, biohybrid systems raise important ethical and biomedical questions, particularly regarding cell sourcing when embryonic or animal-derived cells are used.
